M2 · Fourier Transforms, Delta Functions and Green's Functions

Part 0 — Foundations · Status: draft v1 · Companion notebook: M2_fourier_green_functions.ipynb

Learning goals. After this chapter you should be able to

  • use the Dirac delta function as a limit of ordinary functions, and manipulate δ(g(x))\delta(g(x))δ(g(x)) and
    δ3(r)\delta^3(\mathbf r)δ3(r) in spherical coordinates;
  • Fourier-transform in one and three dimensions with consistent factors of 2π2\pi2π, and compute the
    form factor of a spherical density from a sine transform;
  • normalize continuum states to a delta function, and relate the phase shift to the density of
    states in a large box;
  • evaluate real integrals by closing a contour in the complex plane, using residues and Jordan’s
    lemma;
  • explain what a Green’s function is and how the boundary condition selects it, and turn the
    Schrödinger equation into the Lippmann–Schwinger integral equation;
  • derive the outgoing, incoming and standing-wave Green’s functions of the Helmholtz equation and
    explain the ±iε\pm i\varepsilon±iε prescription;
  • use the Sokhotski–Plemelj formula and the Kramers–Kronig relations that follow from causality.

Prerequisites: M0
(one-dimensional scattering) and M1 (special
functions); complex numbers and Taylor series.

Sources: C&H §4.1.1 (the free-particle Green’s function), §4.1.3 (orthonormality of scattering
states), §4.8.1 (partial-wave Green’s functions) and §10.5.4 (the threshold anomaly); Arfken, Weber
and Harris, the chapters on the delta function, complex variables, Green’s functions and integral
transforms.

How to read this chapter. Chapter 4 rewrites the Schrödinger equation as an integral
equation, and almost every step there uses a tool from this chapter. Sections M2.1–M2.4 collect the
mathematics, M2.5–M2.7 apply it to scattering, and M2.8 previews the dispersion relations of
Chapter 10. The one-dimensional examples use ℏ=1\hbar = 1ℏ=1 and 2m=12m = 12m=1, as in M0, so that E=k2E = k^2E=k2.

M2.1 The Dirac delta function

The Dirac delta function is defined by what it does inside an integral. For every smooth
function fff,

∫−∞∞δ(x−a) f(x) dx=f(a).(M2.1)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(x - a)\,f(x)\,dx = f(a) . \tag{M2.1} ∫−∞∞​δ(x−a)f(x)dx=f(a).(M2.1)

No ordinary function can do this: δ(x)\delta(x)δ(x) would have to vanish for x≠0x \ne 0x=0 and still have unit
area. It is best understood as the limit of a sequence of ordinary functions δε(x)\delta_\varepsilon(x)δε​(x)
of unit area whose width ε\varepsilonε shrinks to zero, called nascent delta functions. Three of
them are used constantly:

δε(x)=e−x2/2ε22π ε,δε(x)=1π εx2+ε2,δε(x)=sin⁡(x/ε)πx=12π∫−1/ε1/εeikx dk.(M2.2)\delta_\varepsilon(x) = \frac{e^{-x^2/2\varepsilon^2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\varepsilon},\qquad \delta_\varepsilon(x) = \frac{1}{\pi}\,\frac{\varepsilon}{x^2 + \varepsilon^2},\qquad \delta_\varepsilon(x) = \frac{\sin(x/\varepsilon)}{\pi x} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-1/\varepsilon}^{1/\varepsilon}e^{ikx}\,dk . \tag{M2.2} δε​(x)=2π​εe−x2/2ε2​,δε​(x)=π1​x2+ε2ε​,δε​(x)=πxsin(x/ε)​=2π1​∫−1/ε1/ε​eikxdk.(M2.2)

The Gaussian is the best behaved. The Lorentzian is what an iεi\varepsiloniε in a denominator produces
(§M2.7). The third, the sinc kernel, is a plane-wave integral cut off at ∣k∣=1/ε|k| = 1/\varepsilon∣k∣=1/ε.
Its limit is the most important identity of this chapter:

∫−∞∞eikx dk=2π δ(x).(M2.3)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{ikx}\,dk = 2\pi\,\delta(x) . \tag{M2.3} ∫−∞∞​eikxdk=2πδ(x).(M2.3)

The sinc kernel does not even tend to zero for x≠0x \ne 0x=0; it oscillates ever faster. The limit makes
sense only inside an integral, where the fast oscillations average out. This is what
“δε→δ\delta_\varepsilon \to \deltaδε​→δ” always means.

How fast is the limit reached? Figure M2.1 compares the three kernels on f(x)=1/(1+x2)f(x) = 1/(1 + x^2)f(x)=1/(1+x2),
for which every integral is known exactly.

  • Gaussian. Expand fff about the origin. The odd terms cancel, and the error is
    12f′′(0) ε2+O(ε4)\frac12f''(0)\,\varepsilon^2 + O(\varepsilon^4)21​f′′(0)ε2+O(ε4), here −ε2-\varepsilon^2−ε2.
  • Lorentzian. Its tails fall only as ε/πx2\varepsilon/\pi x^2ε/πx2, so its second moment is infinite and the
    error is of first order in ε\varepsilonε. For this fff it is exactly 1−1/(1+ε)1 - 1/(1 + \varepsilon)1−1/(1+ε).
  • Sinc. It keeps exactly the Fourier components of fff with ∣k∣<1/ε|k| < 1/\varepsilon∣k∣<1/ε (§M2.2), so the
    error is the weight of the components it drops, 12π∫∣k∣>1/εf~(k) dk\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{|k|>1/\varepsilon}\tilde f(k)\,dk2π1​∫∣k∣>1/ε​f~​(k)dk.
    Here f~(k)=πe−∣k∣\tilde f(k) = \pi e^{-|k|}f~​(k)=πe−∣k∣, and the error e−1/εe^{-1/\varepsilon}e−1/ε is exponentially small.

At ε=0.1\varepsilon = 0.1ε=0.1 the errors are 9.7×10−39.7\times10^{-3}9.7×10−3, 9.1×10−29.1\times10^{-2}9.1×10−2 and 4.5×10−54.5\times10^{-5}4.5×10−5.
The slow Lorentzian will return in §M2.7, where the iεi\varepsiloniε of scattering theory produces
exactly this kernel.

Rules. A change of variables in (M2.1) gives

δ(−x)=δ(x),x δ(x)=0,δ(ax)=δ(x)∣a∣,δ(g(x))=∑iδ(x−xi)∣g′(xi)∣,(M2.4)\delta(-x) = \delta(x),\qquad x\,\delta(x) = 0,\qquad \delta(ax) = \frac{\delta(x)}{|a|},\qquad \delta\big(g(x)\big) = \sum_i\frac{\delta(x - x_i)}{|g'(x_i)|}, \tag{M2.4} δ(−x)=δ(x),xδ(x)=0,δ(ax)=∣a∣δ(x)​,δ(g(x))=i∑​∣g′(xi​)∣δ(x−xi​)​,(M2.4)

where the xix_ixi​ are the simple zeros of ggg. Energy conservation is the typical application: for
k>0k > 0k>0, δ(E−ℏ2k2/2μ)=(μ/ℏ2kE) δ(k−kE)\delta(E - \hbar^2k^2/2\mu) = (\mu/\hbar^2k_E)\,\delta(k - k_E)δ(E−ℏ2k2/2μ)=(μ/ℏ2kE​)δ(k−kE​) with
kE=2μE/ℏk_E = \sqrt{2\mu E}/\hbarkE​=2μE​/ℏ. The derivative of the delta function is defined by integrating by parts,
∫δ′(x) f(x) dx=−f′(0)\int\delta'(x)\,f(x)\,dx = -f'(0)∫δ′(x)f(x)dx=−f′(0), and the unit step function θ(x)\theta(x)θ(x) has
θ′(x)=δ(x)\theta'(x) = \delta(x)θ′(x)=δ(x).

Three dimensions. δ3(r−r′)=δ(x−x′) δ(y−y′) δ(z−z′)\delta^3(\mathbf r - \mathbf r') = \delta(x - x')\,\delta(y - y')\,\delta(z - z')δ3(r−r′)=δ(x−x′)δ(y−y′)δ(z−z′).
In spherical coordinates the volume element is r2 dr dΩr^2\,dr\,d\Omegar2drdΩ, so

δ3(r−r′)=δ(r−r′)r2 δ(Ω−Ω′),δ(Ω−Ω′)=δ(cos⁡θ−cos⁡θ′) δ(ϕ−ϕ′)=∑l,mYlm(Ω) Ylm∗(Ω′).(M2.5)\delta^3(\mathbf r - \mathbf r') = \frac{\delta(r - r')}{r^2}\,\delta(\Omega - \Omega'),\qquad \delta(\Omega - \Omega') = \delta(\cos\theta - \cos\theta')\,\delta(\phi - \phi') = \sum_{l,m}Y_{lm}(\Omega)\,Y^*_{lm}(\Omega') . \tag{M2.5} δ3(r−r′)=r2δ(r−r′)​δ(Ω−Ω′),δ(Ω−Ω′)=δ(cosθ−cosθ′)δ(ϕ−ϕ′)=l,m∑​Ylm​(Ω)Ylm∗​(Ω′).(M2.5)

The last form is the completeness of the spherical harmonics (M1.12). Finally, the potential of a
point charge obeys

∇21r=−4π δ3(r).(M2.6)\nabla^2\frac{1}{r} = -4\pi\,\delta^3(\mathbf r) . \tag{M2.6} ∇2r1​=−4πδ3(r).(M2.6)

For r≠0r \ne 0r=0 the left side vanishes, as (M1.1) shows. Integrate over a small ball around the origin
and use Gauss’s theorem: the flux of ∇(1/r)=−r^/r2\nabla(1/r) = -\hat{\mathbf r}/r^2∇(1/r)=−r^/r2 through a sphere of any radius
is −4π-4\pi−4π. Equation (M2.6) is the simplest Green’s function, that of §M2.6 at k=0k = 0k=0.

M2.2 Fourier transforms in one and three dimensions

We put all factors of 2π2\pi2π into the inverse transform:

f~(k)=∫−∞∞e−ikxf(x) dx,f(x)=∫−∞∞eikx f~(k) dk2π.(M2.7)\tilde f(k) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-ikx}f(x)\,dx,\qquad f(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{ikx}\,\tilde f(k)\,\frac{dk}{2\pi} . \tag{M2.7} f~​(k)=∫−∞∞​e−ikxf(x)dx,f(x)=∫−∞∞​eikxf~​(k)2πdk​.(M2.7)

Inserting the first formula into the second and using (M2.3) confirms the pair. In three dimensions

f~(q)=∫e−iq⋅rf(r) d3r,f(r)=∫eiq⋅r f~(q) d3q(2π)3,∫eiq⋅r d3r=(2π)3 δ3(q).(M2.8)\tilde f(\mathbf q) = \int e^{-i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r}f(\mathbf r)\,d^3r,\qquad f(\mathbf r) = \int e^{i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r}\,\tilde f(\mathbf q)\,\frac{d^3q}{(2\pi)^3},\qquad \int e^{i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r}\,d^3r = (2\pi)^3\,\delta^3(\mathbf q) . \tag{M2.8} f~​(q)=∫e−iq⋅rf(r)d3r,f(r)=∫eiq⋅rf~​(q)(2π)3d3q​,∫eiq⋅rd3r=(2π)3δ3(q).(M2.8)

This is the convention for potentials and densities used throughout these notes and in
scatlib.fourier. Wave functions are normalized separately (§M2.3). Four properties do most of the
work:

derivatives:∇→iq,∇2→−q2,convolution:∫f(r−r′) g(r′) d3r′  →  f~(q) g~(q),Parseval:∫∣f∣2 d3r=∫∣f~∣2 d3q(2π)3,widths:Δr Δq∼1.(M2.9)\begin{aligned} &\text{derivatives:} && \nabla \to i\mathbf q,\qquad \nabla^2 \to -q^2,\\ &\text{convolution:} && \int f(\mathbf r - \mathbf r')\,g(\mathbf r')\,d^3r' \;\to\; \tilde f(\mathbf q)\,\tilde g(\mathbf q),\\ &\text{Parseval:} && \int|f|^2\,d^3r = \int|\tilde f|^2\,\frac{d^3q}{(2\pi)^3},\\ &\text{widths:} && \Delta r\,\Delta q \sim 1 . \end{aligned} \tag{M2.9} ​derivatives:convolution:Parseval:widths:​​∇→iq,∇2→−q2,∫f(r−r′)g(r′)d3r′→f~​(q)g~​(q),∫∣f∣2d3r=∫∣f~​∣2(2π)3d3q​,ΔrΔq∼1.​(M2.9)

The first turns a differential equation with constant coefficients into an algebraic one; §M2.6 uses
it to find the Green’s function. The last is the uncertainty principle: a feature of size Δr\Delta rΔr
in fff shows up at q∼1/Δrq \sim 1/\Delta rq∼1/Δr in f~\tilde ff~​.

Spherically symmetric functions. If fff depends only on rrr, then f~\tilde ff~​ depends only on
q=∣q∣q = |\mathbf q|q=∣q∣. Take q\mathbf qq along the zzz axis. The angular integral is elementary,
∫e−iqrcos⁡θ dΩ=4πsin⁡(qr)/qr=4πj0(qr)\int e^{-iqr\cos\theta}\,d\Omega = 4\pi\sin(qr)/qr = 4\pi j_0(qr)∫e−iqrcosθdΩ=4πsin(qr)/qr=4πj0​(qr), and

f~(q)=4π∫0∞r2f(r) j0(qr) dr=4πq∫0∞r f(r)sin⁡(qr) dr.(M2.10)\tilde f(q) = 4\pi\int_0^\infty r^2f(r)\,j_0(qr)\,dr = \frac{4\pi}{q}\int_0^\infty r\,f(r)\sin(qr)\,dr . \tag{M2.10} f~​(q)=4π∫0∞​r2f(r)j0​(qr)dr=q4π​∫0∞​rf(r)sin(qr)dr.(M2.10)

A three-dimensional transform has become a one-dimensional sine transform. For
f(r) Ylm(r^)f(r)\,Y_{lm}(\hat{\mathbf r})f(r)Ylm​(r^) the same steps, with the plane-wave expansion (M1.20), give a
transform with jlj_ljl​ in place of j0j_0j0​. Three transforms recur throughout these notes:

e−μrr  →  4πq2+μ2,e−r2/2σ2(2πσ2)3/2  →  e−q2σ2/2,3 θ(R−r)4πR3  →  3 (sin⁡qR−qRcos⁡qR)(qR)3.(M2.11)\frac{e^{-\mu r}}{r}\;\to\;\frac{4\pi}{q^2 + \mu^2},\qquad \frac{e^{-r^2/2\sigma^2}}{(2\pi\sigma^2)^{3/2}}\;\to\;e^{-q^2\sigma^2/2},\qquad \frac{3\,\theta(R - r)}{4\pi R^3}\;\to\;\frac{3\,(\sin qR - qR\cos qR)}{(qR)^3} . \tag{M2.11} re−μr​→q2+μ24π​,(2πσ2)3/2e−r2/2σ2​→e−q2σ2/2,4πR33θ(R−r)​→(qR)33(sinqR−qRcosqR)​.(M2.11)

The first is the Yukawa function. Its limit μ→0\mu \to 0μ→0 gives the transform of the Coulomb potential,
4π/q24\pi/q^24π/q2.

Form factors. For a density normalized to ∫ρ d3r=1\int\rho\,d^3r = 1∫ρd3r=1, the transform F(q)=ρ~(q)F(q) = \tilde\rho(q)F(q)=ρ~​(q)
is called the form factor. It is what electron scattering measures. In the Born approximation
(Chapter 5), the cross section for scattering from a nucleus with charge density Ze ρ(r)Ze\,\rho(r)Zeρ(r) is that
of a point charge times ∣F(q)∣2|F(q)|^2∣F(q)∣2, at the momentum transfer q=2ksin⁡(θ/2)q = 2k\sin(\theta/2)q=2ksin(θ/2). Expanding
j0(qr)=1−(qr)2/6+(qr)4/120−…j_0(qr) = 1 - (qr)^2/6 + (qr)^4/120 - \dotsj0​(qr)=1−(qr)2/6+(qr)4/120−… in (M2.10) gives

F(q)=1−q2⟨r2⟩6+q4⟨r4⟩120−…,(M2.12)F(q) = 1 - \frac{q^2\langle r^2\rangle}{6} + \frac{q^4\langle r^4\rangle}{120} - \dots , \tag{M2.12} F(q)=1−6q2⟨r2⟩​+120q4⟨r4⟩​−…,(M2.12)

so the slope at q=0q = 0q=0 measures the rms radius, whatever the shape of the density.

Figure M2.2 compares three densities with the same rms radius:

  • a Fermi distribution ρ∝[1+e(r−c)/a]−1\rho \propto [1 + e^{(r - c)/a}]^{-1}ρ∝[1+e(r−c)/a]−1 with c=6.62c = 6.62c=6.62 fm and a=0.55a = 0.55a=0.55 fm,
    close to the measured charge density of ²⁰⁸Pb, whose rms radius is 5.520 fm;
  • a uniform sphere, which needs R=5/3 rrms=7.127R = \sqrt{5/3}\,r_{\rm rms} = 7.127R=5/3​rrms​=7.127 fm;
  • a Gaussian, which needs σ=rrms/3=3.187\sigma = r_{\rm rms}/\sqrt3 = 3.187σ=rrms​/3​=3.187 fm.

The numerical sine transform reproduces the closed forms (M2.11) to 9×10−59\times10^{-5}9×10−5 for the uniform
sphere and 1.2×10−51.2\times10^{-5}1.2×10−5 for the Gaussian. At q=0.1q = 0.1q=0.1 fm⁻¹ the Fermi density has
1−F=0.049801 - F = 0.049801−F=0.04980. The q2q^2q2 term of (M2.12) gives 0.05079, and adding the q4q^4q4 term brings it to
0.04979.

The figure is a lesson in reading momentum space:

  • Sharp edges make diffraction minima. The uniform sphere has zeros where tan⁡qR=qR\tan qR = qRtanqR=qR, at
    qR=4.493, 7.725, 10.904qR = 4.493,\ 7.725,\ 10.904qR=4.493, 7.725, 10.904, i.e. q=0.630, 1.084, 1.530q = 0.630,\ 1.084,\ 1.530q=0.630, 1.084, 1.530 fm⁻¹. The Fermi distribution has
    minima at q=0.665, 1.145, 1.62q = 0.665,\ 1.145,\ 1.62q=0.665, 1.145, 1.62 fm⁻¹, so the minima measure the size of the nucleus. They lie
    slightly further out because the diffuse surface adds to ⟨r2⟩\langle r^2\rangle⟨r2⟩: at equal rms radius,
    the sharp-edged core of the Fermi distribution is smaller.
  • The surface sets the fall-off. The maxima of the uniform sphere’s form factor decay only as
    q−2q^{-2}q−2, the signature of a discontinuity. Those of the Fermi form factor decay exponentially,
    roughly as e−πqae^{-\pi qa}e−πqa, at a rate fixed by the diffuseness aaa.
  • No flat interior, no minima. The Gaussian has neither a sharp edge nor a flat interior. Its form
    factor falls monotonically and much faster.

Hofstadter’s electron-scattering experiments of the 1950s used exactly this reasoning to establish
the shape of nuclear charge densities.

M2.3 Normalizing continuum states

A plane wave is not square integrable, so it cannot be normalized to 1. It is normalized to a delta
function instead. By (M2.8),

⟨r∣k⟩=eik⋅r(2π)3/2:⟨k∣k′⟩=δ3(k−k′),∫∣k⟩⟨k∣ d3k=1.(M2.13)\langle\mathbf r|\mathbf k\rangle = \frac{e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}}{(2\pi)^{3/2}}:\qquad \langle\mathbf k|\mathbf k'\rangle = \delta^3(\mathbf k - \mathbf k'),\qquad \int|\mathbf k\rangle\langle\mathbf k|\,d^3k = 1 . \tag{M2.13} ⟨r∣k⟩=(2π)3/2eik⋅r​:⟨k∣k′⟩=δ3(k−k′),∫∣k⟩⟨k∣d3k=1.(M2.13)

This is the normalization used from Chapter 4 on. The completeness relation says that any wave
packet can be expanded in plane waves. With a potential, the scattering states and the bound states
together form a complete set; the counting argument below shows how they share the states.

Two other normalizations are common. Energy normalization, ⟨E∣E′⟩=δ(E−E′)\langle E|E'\rangle = \delta(E - E')⟨E∣E′⟩=δ(E−E′),
is convenient for resonances and for RRR-matrix theory. Box normalization puts the system in a
cube of side LLL with periodic boundary conditions. The wave numbers are then discrete,
k=2πn/L\mathbf k = 2\pi\mathbf n/Lk=2πn/L, the states eik⋅r/L3/2e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}/L^{3/2}eik⋅r/L3/2 are normalized to 1,
and sums over states become integrals weighted by the density of states:

∑k  ⟶  L3(2π)3∫d3k.(M2.14)\sum_{\mathbf k}\;\longrightarrow\;\frac{L^3}{(2\pi)^3}\int d^3k . \tag{M2.14} k∑​⟶(2π)3L3​∫d3k.(M2.14)

Physical results never depend on LLL, which cancels between the normalization and the density of
states. This is the cleanest route to Fermi’s golden rule and to cross sections.

Radial functions. The free radial solutions of Chapter 2 obey

∫0∞j^l(kr) j^l(k′r) dr=π2 δ(k−k′)(k, k′>0).(M2.15)\int_0^\infty\hat j_l(kr)\,\hat j_l(k'r)\,dr = \frac{\pi}{2}\,\delta(k - k')\qquad(k,\ k' > 0) . \tag{M2.15} ∫0∞​j^​l​(kr)j^​l​(k′r)dr=2π​δ(k−k′)(k, k′>0).(M2.15)

For l=0l = 0l=0 this is ∫0∞sin⁡kr sin⁡k′r dr\int_0^\infty\sin kr\,\sin k'r\,dr∫0∞​sinkrsink′rdr. Write the product as
12[cos⁡(k−k′)r−cos⁡(k+k′)r]\frac12[\cos(k - k')r - \cos(k + k')r]21​[cos(k−k′)r−cos(k+k′)r] and use (M2.3). The second term gives δ(k+k′)\delta(k + k')δ(k+k′), which
vanishes for positive kkk and k′k'k′. The same normalization holds for scattering solutions with unit
asymptotic amplitude, ul→sin⁡(kr−lπ/2+δl)u_l \to \sin(kr - l\pi/2 + \delta_l)ul​→sin(kr−lπ/2+δl​). The delta function comes only from
r→∞r \to \inftyr→∞, where the amplitude matters but the phase shift does not.

Box states and phase shifts. Now enclose an s-wave problem in a sphere of radius RboxR_{\rm box}Rbox​,
with u(Rbox)=0u(R_{\rm box}) = 0u(Rbox​)=0. If the box is larger than the range of the potential, u∝sin⁡(kr+δ0)u \propto \sin(kr + \delta_0)u∝sin(kr+δ0​) near the wall, and the allowed wave numbers satisfy

knRbox+δ0(kn)=nπ.(M2.16)k_nR_{\rm box} + \delta_0(k_n) = n\pi . \tag{M2.16} kn​Rbox​+δ0​(kn​)=nπ.(M2.16)

Here nnn also counts the bound states. By Levinson’s theorem, δ0(0)=nbπ\delta_0(0) = n_b\piδ0​(0)=nb​π, so the lowest
continuum level has n=nb+1n = n_b + 1n=nb​+1. Without the potential, kn(0)Rbox=nπk_n^{(0)}R_{\rm box} = n\pikn(0)​Rbox​=nπ, so each level
is shifted by

Δkn=kn−kn(0)=−δ0(kn)Rbox,(M2.17)\Delta k_n = k_n - k_n^{(0)} = -\frac{\delta_0(k_n)}{R_{\rm box}} , \tag{M2.17} Δkn​=kn​−kn(0)​=−Rbox​δ0​(kn​)​,(M2.17)

downward for an attractive potential (δ0>0\delta_0 > 0δ0​>0) and upward for a repulsive one. A small shift
measured in a large box gives the phase shift. Worked out for periodic boxes, the same idea is how
lattice QCD extracts hadron–hadron phase shifts from energy levels in a finite volume (Lüscher’s
method).

Counting states. By (M2.16), the number of continuum levels below kkk is the integer part of
[kRbox+δ0(k)]/π[kR_{\rm box} + \delta_0(k)]/\pi[kRbox​+δ0​(k)]/π minus nbn_bnb​; without the potential it is the integer part of
kRbox/πkR_{\rm box}/\pikRbox​/π. Averaged over one level spacing π/Rbox\pi/R_{\rm box}π/Rbox​, the difference is

N(k)−N0(k)≃δ0(k)π−nb,(M2.18)N(k) - N_0(k) \simeq \frac{\delta_0(k)}{\pi} - n_b , \tag{M2.18} N(k)−N0​(k)≃πδ0​(k)​−nb​,(M2.18)

and the change in the density of states is

Δρ(k)=1π dδ0dk,(M2.19)\Delta\rho(k) = \frac{1}{\pi}\,\frac{d\delta_0}{dk} , \tag{M2.19} Δρ(k)=π1​dkdδ0​​,(M2.19)

independent of the size of the box. Summed over partial waves with weights 2l+12l + 12l+1, this is the
Beth–Uhlenbeck formula for the effect of interactions on the second virial coefficient of a gas.
As k→∞k \to \inftyk→∞, δ0→0\delta_0 \to 0δ0​→0 and N−N0→−nbN - N_0 \to -n_bN−N0​→−nb​: the potential has moved exactly nbn_bnb​
states out of the continuum into bound states, and the total number of states is unchanged. This is
Levinson’s theorem (2.32) seen as state counting, and it explains why the phase shift must start at
nbπn_b\pinb​π.

M2.4 A complex-analysis toolkit

Most integrals of scattering theory are evaluated in the complex plane. Five facts are enough.

Analytic functions. A function f(z)f(z)f(z) is analytic in a region if it has a complex derivative
there. Polynomials, eze^zez, and ratios of analytic functions away from the zeros of the denominator are
analytic.

Cauchy’s theorem. The integral of an analytic function around a closed contour vanishes. A
contour may therefore be deformed freely, as long as it does not cross a singularity.

Poles and residues. Near an isolated singularity z0z_0z0​, fff has a Laurent series
f=∑n=−∞∞an(z−z0)nf = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}a_n(z - z_0)^nf=∑n=−∞∞​an​(z−z0​)n. If the most negative power is −m-m−m, z0z_0z0​ is a pole of
order mmm, and the coefficient a−1a_{-1}a−1​ is the residue. For a simple pole of f=g/hf = g/hf=g/h, with
h(z0)=0h(z_0) = 0h(z0​)=0 and h′(z0)≠0h'(z_0) \ne 0h′(z0​)=0,

Res⁡z0f=g(z0)h′(z0).(M2.20)\operatorname{Res}_{z_0}f = \frac{g(z_0)}{h'(z_0)} . \tag{M2.20} Resz0​​f=h′(z0​)g(z0​)​.(M2.20)

The residue theorem. For a closed contour CCC traversed counterclockwise,

∮Cf(z) dz=2πi∑poles inside CRes⁡f.(M2.21)\oint_C f(z)\,dz = 2\pi i\sum_{\text{poles inside }C}\operatorname{Res}f . \tag{M2.21} ∮C​f(z)dz=2πipoles inside C∑​Resf.(M2.21)

Jordan’s lemma. Let g(q)→0g(q) \to 0g(q)→0 as ∣q∣→∞|q| \to \infty∣q∣→∞ in the upper half plane, and let r>0r > 0r>0.
Then the integral of g(q) eiqrg(q)\,e^{iqr}g(q)eiqr over a large semicircle in the upper half plane vanishes as its
radius goes to infinity, because ∣eiqr∣=e−r Im q|e^{iqr}| = e^{-r\,\mathrm{Im}\,q}∣eiqr∣=e−rImq is exponentially small there.
Closing the real axis with that semicircle gives, for r>0r > 0r>0,

∫−∞∞g(q) eiqr dq=2πi∑Im qj>0Res⁡qj ⁣[g(q) eiqr].(M2.22)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}g(q)\,e^{iqr}\,dq = 2\pi i\sum_{\mathrm{Im}\,q_j > 0}\operatorname{Res}_{q_j}\!\big[g(q)\,e^{iqr}\big] . \tag{M2.22} ∫−∞∞​g(q)eiqrdq=2πiImqj​>0∑​Resqj​​[g(q)eiqr].(M2.22)

For r<0r < 0r<0 the contour must be closed in the lower half plane instead, clockwise, which brings a
minus sign. The rule to remember: close the contour on the side where the exponential decays.

Example. Take g=1/(q2+a2)g = 1/(q^2 + a^2)g=1/(q2+a2) with a>0a > 0a>0. Its poles are at q=±iaq = \pm iaq=±ia. Only +ia+ia+ia lies in
the upper half plane, and by (M2.20) the residue there is e−ar/2iae^{-ar}/2iae−ar/2ia. Taking the real part,

∫−∞∞cos⁡qrq2+a2 dq=πa e−ar(r>0).(M2.23)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\cos qr}{q^2 + a^2}\,dq = \frac{\pi}{a}\,e^{-ar}\qquad(r > 0) . \tag{M2.23} ∫−∞∞​q2+a2cosqr​dq=aπ​e−ar(r>0).(M2.23)

The notebook confirms this by brute-force quadrature to 3×10−73\times10^{-7}3×10−7, the error of cutting the
integral off at ∣q∣=4000|q| = 4000∣q∣=4000. Keep this example in mind. Its three-dimensional version produces the
Yukawa function of (M2.11). And if we let a→ε∓ika \to \varepsilon \mp ika→ε∓ik, the poles approach the real axis
at q=±kq = \pm kq=±k, and e−are^{-ar}e−ar becomes the spherical wave e±ikre^{\pm ikr}e±ikr. Section M2.6 shows how to
handle poles that sit on the path of integration.

M2.5 Green’s functions: the idea

Consider a linear equation with a source, L u(x)=s(x)\mathcal L\,u(x) = s(x)Lu(x)=s(x), where L\mathcal LL is a
differential operator, together with boundary conditions. The Green’s function is the response to
a point source, with the same boundary conditions:

L G(x,x′)=δ(x−x′)⟹u(x)=∫G(x,x′) s(x′) dx′.(M2.24)\mathcal L\,G(x, x') = \delta(x - x')\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad u(x) = \int G(x, x')\,s(x')\,dx' . \tag{M2.24} LG(x,x′)=δ(x−x′)⟹u(x)=∫G(x,x′)s(x′)dx′.(M2.24)

Apply L\mathcal LL to the integral and use (M2.1) to check this. Any source is a superposition of
point sources, and by linearity the response is the same superposition of point responses. Two
Green’s functions of the same operator differ by a solution of the homogeneous equation
L u=0\mathcal L\,u = 0Lu=0. The boundary conditions select the Green’s function.

One dimension. Take L=d2/dx2+k2\mathcal L = d^2/dx^2 + k^2L=d2/dx2+k2 on the whole line. Away from x′x'x′, GGG solves
the free equation, so on each side it is a combination of eikxe^{ikx}eikx and e−ikxe^{-ikx}e−ikx. Integrating the
equation across x=x′x = x'x=x′ shows that GGG is continuous there and that its slope jumps by 1. Demanding
waves that travel away from the source on both sides fixes G+G^{+}G+ below. G−G^-G− has incoming waves
on both sides, and GP=12(G++G−)G^P = \frac12(G^+ + G^-)GP=21​(G++G−) is a standing wave:

G+(x,x′)=eik∣x−x′∣2ik,G−(x,x′)=−e−ik∣x−x′∣2ik,GP(x,x′)=sin⁡k∣x−x′∣2k.(M2.25)G^{+}(x, x') = \frac{e^{ik|x - x'|}}{2ik},\qquad G^{-}(x, x') = -\frac{e^{-ik|x - x'|}}{2ik},\qquad G^{P}(x, x') = \frac{\sin k|x - x'|}{2k} . \tag{M2.25} G+(x,x′)=2ikeik∣x−x′∣​,G−(x,x′)=−2ike−ik∣x−x′∣​,GP(x,x′)=2ksink∣x−x′∣​.(M2.25)

Each has the required unit jump in slope.

The Lippmann–Schwinger equation. With ℏ=2m=1\hbar = 2m = 1ℏ=2m=1, the Schrödinger equation is
ψ′′+k2ψ=Vψ\psi'' + k^2\psi = V\psiψ′′+k2ψ=Vψ. Treat the right side as a source. The solution with an incident wave
eikxe^{ikx}eikx and only outgoing scattered waves is

ψ(x)=eikx+∫−∞∞G+(x,x′) V(x′) ψ(x′) dx′.(M2.26)\psi(x) = e^{ikx} + \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}G^{+}(x, x')\,V(x')\,\psi(x')\,dx' . \tag{M2.26} ψ(x)=eikx+∫−∞∞​G+(x,x′)V(x′)ψ(x′)dx′.(M2.26)

This integral equation is equivalent to the differential equation plus the scattering boundary
conditions. The homogeneous term fixes the incident wave, and G+G^+G+ guarantees that nothing else comes
in. Far to the right of the potential, ∣x−x′∣=x−x′|x - x'| = x - x'∣x−x′∣=x−x′; far to the left, ∣x−x′∣=x′−x|x - x'| = x' - x∣x−x′∣=x′−x.
Comparing with ψ→t eikx\psi \to t\,e^{ikx}ψ→teikx and ψ→eikx+r e−ikx\psi \to e^{ikx} + r\,e^{-ikx}ψ→eikx+re−ikx (M0) gives

t=1+12ik∫e−ikx′ V(x′) ψ(x′) dx′,r=12ik∫eikx′ V(x′) ψ(x′) dx′.(M2.27)t = 1 + \frac{1}{2ik}\int e^{-ikx'}\,V(x')\,\psi(x')\,dx',\qquad r = \frac{1}{2ik}\int e^{ikx'}\,V(x')\,\psi(x')\,dx' . \tag{M2.27} t=1+2ik1​∫e−ikx′V(x′)ψ(x′)dx′,r=2ik1​∫eikx′V(x′)ψ(x′)dx′.(M2.27)

The amplitudes need ψ\psiψ only where V≠0V \ne 0V=0.

The Born approximation. If VVV is weak, replace ψ\psiψ by eikxe^{ikx}eikx inside the integral:

rB=12ik∫e2ikx V(x) dx=V~(−2k)2ik.(M2.28)r_B = \frac{1}{2ik}\int e^{2ikx}\,V(x)\,dx = \frac{\tilde V(-2k)}{2ik} . \tag{M2.28} rB​=2ik1​∫e2ikxV(x)dx=2ikV~(−2k)​.(M2.28)

Reflection probes the Fourier component of the potential at the momentum transfer 2k2k2k, the change
of momentum when the particle turns around. For the Eckart barrier VB/cosh⁡2xV_B/\cosh^2xVB​/cosh2x this gives
rB=−iπVB/sinh⁡πkr_B = -i\pi V_B/\sinh\pi krB​=−iπVB​/sinhπk.

Solving it numerically. Replace the integral by a quadrature rule with nodes xjx_jxj​ and weights
wjw_jwj​. Then (M2.26) becomes a linear system,

∑j[δij−G+(xi,xj) V(xj) wj] ψ(xj)=eikxi,(M2.29)\sum_j\big[\delta_{ij} - G^{+}(x_i, x_j)\,V(x_j)\,w_j\big]\,\psi(x_j) = e^{ikx_i} , \tag{M2.29} j∑​[δij​−G+(xi​,xj​)V(xj​)wj​]ψ(xj​)=eikxi​,(M2.29)

the Nyström method. scatlib.onedim.lippmann_schwinger solves it with the trapezoidal rule on
801 points in −10≤x≤10-10 \le x \le 10−10≤x≤10. For two Eckart barriers it reproduces the exact reflection
probability (M0.11) to 3.7×10−53.7\times10^{-5}3.7×10−5 (VB=1V_B = 1VB​=1) and 3.9×10−63.9\times10^{-6}3.9×10−6 (VB=0.2V_B = 0.2VB​=0.2) over
0.08≤E≤60.08 \le E \le 60.08≤E≤6 (Fig. M2.5a). At E=0.6E = 0.6E=0.6 the solution has ∣r∣2+∣t∣2=1.000000|r|^2 + |t|^2 = 1.000000∣r∣2+∣t∣2=1.000000, and far to
the right ∣ψ∣2|\psi|^2∣ψ∣2 equals ∣t∣2=0.354704|t|^2 = 0.354704∣t∣2=0.354704. The boundary conditions come out of the integral
equation without ever being imposed.

The Born approximation teaches two lessons here. First, it can violate unitarity: for VB=1V_B = 1VB​=1, RBR_BRB​
exceeds 1 below E≈0.35E \approx 0.35E≈0.35, while at E=0.5E = 0.5E=0.5 it is only 0.65 of the exact value. Second, and
more surprising, it does not improve at high energy. Both RB=π2VB2/sinh⁡2πkR_B = \pi^2V_B^2/\sinh^2\pi kRB​=π2VB2​/sinh2πk and the
exact RRR fall as 1/sinh⁡2πk1/\sinh^2\pi k1/sinh2πk, and their ratio tends to the constant
π2VB2/cosh⁡2 ⁣(πVB−1/4)\pi^2V_B^2/\cosh^2\!\big(\pi\sqrt{V_B - 1/4}\big)π2VB2​/cosh2(πVB​−1/4​) (with cos in place of cosh for VB<1/4V_B < 1/4VB​<1/4). That
is 0.17 for VB=1V_B = 1VB​=1 and 0.68 for VB=0.2V_B = 0.2VB​=0.2. Reflection from a smooth barrier at high energy is
exponentially small, and every order of the Born series contributes with the same exponential factor.
Only the strength VBV_BVB​, in units of ℏ2/2md2\hbar^2/2md^2ℏ2/2md2, decides how good the first term is. Chapter 5
returns to the validity of the Born approximation.

M2.6 The Green’s function of the Helmholtz equation

In three dimensions the Schrödinger equation at energy E=ℏ2k2/2μE = \hbar^2k^2/2\muE=ℏ2k2/2μ reads
(∇2+k2)ψ=Uψ(\nabla^2 + k^2)\psi = U\psi(∇2+k2)ψ=Uψ, with U=2μV/ℏ2U = 2\mu V/\hbar^2U=2μV/ℏ2 as in Chapter 2. Its Green’s function solves
the Helmholtz equation with a point source:

(∇2+k2) G(r−r′)=δ3(r−r′).(M2.30)(\nabla^2 + k^2)\,G(\mathbf r - \mathbf r') = \delta^3(\mathbf r - \mathbf r') . \tag{M2.30} (∇2+k2)G(r−r′)=δ3(r−r′).(M2.30)

Free space is uniform, so GGG depends only on r−r′\mathbf r - \mathbf r'r−r′, and we may set
r′=0\mathbf r' = 0r′=0. Fourier transforming with (M2.9) gives (k2−q2) G~(q)=1(k^2 - q^2)\,\tilde G(\mathbf q) = 1(k2−q2)G~(q)=1, so

G(r)=∫eiq⋅rk2−q2 d3q(2π)3=14π2ir∫−∞∞q eiqrk2−q2 dq.(M2.31)G(\mathbf r) = \int\frac{e^{i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r}}{k^2 - q^2}\,\frac{d^3q}{(2\pi)^3} = \frac{1}{4\pi^2ir}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{q\,e^{iqr}}{k^2 - q^2}\,dq . \tag{M2.31} G(r)=∫k2−q2eiq⋅r​(2π)3d3q​=4π2ir1​∫−∞∞​k2−q2qeiqr​dq.(M2.31)

For the second form, do the angular integral as in (M2.10). This leaves
12π2r∫0∞qsin⁡qr/(k2−q2) dq\frac{1}{2\pi^2r}\int_0^\infty q\sin qr/(k^2 - q^2)\,dq2π2r1​∫0∞​qsinqr/(k2−q2)dq. The integrand is even in qqq, so extend
the integral to the whole axis and write sin⁡qr\sin qrsinqr in exponentials; the e−iqre^{-iqr}e−iqr term equals the
eiqre^{iqr}eiqr term after q→−qq \to -qq→−q.

As it stands, (M2.31) is not defined: the poles at q=±kq = \pm kq=±k lie on the path of integration. This
is not a defect of the method. Equation (M2.30) alone does not determine GGG, since any solution of
the free equation can be added to it. A prescription for passing the poles is a choice of boundary
condition.

Outgoing waves. Replace k2k^2k2 by k2+iεk^2 + i\varepsilonk2+iε, and let ε→0+\varepsilon \to 0^+ε→0+ at the end.
The poles move to q=±(k+iε)q = \pm(k + i\varepsilon)q=±(k+iε), where ε/2k\varepsilon/2kε/2k has been renamed ε\varepsilonε.
For r>0r > 0r>0 close the contour in the upper half plane; it encloses only q=k+iεq = k + i\varepsilonq=k+iε
(Fig. M2.4a). With k2−q2=−(q−k)(q+k)k^2 - q^2 = -(q - k)(q + k)k2−q2=−(q−k)(q+k), (M2.20) gives the residue −12eikr-\frac12e^{ikr}−21​eikr, and
(M2.22) gives the integral −iπ eikr-i\pi\,e^{ikr}−iπeikr. Incoming waves follow in the same way from

G(±)(r−r′)=−e±ik∣r−r′∣4π∣r−r′∣.(M2.32)G^{(\pm)}(\mathbf r - \mathbf r') = -\frac{e^{\pm ik|\mathbf r - \mathbf r'|}}{4\pi|\mathbf r - \mathbf r'|} . \tag{M2.32} G(±)(r−r′)=−4π∣r−r′∣e±ik∣r−r′∣​.(M2.32)

With the time dependence e−iωte^{-i\omega t}e−iωt, G(+)G^{(+)}G(+) describes spherical waves running away from the

GP=12(G(+)+G(−))=−cos⁡kr4πr,G(+)−G(−)=−i2π sin⁡krr.(M2.33)G^{P} = \tfrac12\big(G^{(+)} + G^{(-)}\big) = -\frac{\cos kr}{4\pi r},\qquad G^{(+)} - G^{(-)} = -\frac{i}{2\pi}\,\frac{\sin kr}{r} . \tag{M2.33} GP=21​(G(+)+G(−))=−4πrcoskr​,G(+)−G(−)=−2πi​rsinkr​.(M2.33)

with the scattering amplitude

f(k′,k)=−14π∫e−ik′⋅r′ U(r′) ψ(+)(r′) d3r′  ≈  −14π U~(k′−k).(M2.35)f(\mathbf k', \mathbf k) = -\frac{1}{4\pi}\int e^{-i\mathbf k'\cdot\mathbf r'}\,U(\mathbf r')\,\psi^{(+)}(\mathbf r')\,d^3r' \;\approx\; -\frac{1}{4\pi}\,\tilde U(\mathbf k' - \mathbf k) . \tag{M2.35} f(k′,k)=−4π1​∫e−ik′⋅r′U(r′)ψ(+)(r′)d3r′≈−4π1​U~(k′−k).(M2.35)

The second form is the first Born approximation, obtained with ψ(+)→eik⋅r\psi^{(+)} \to e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}ψ(+)→eik⋅r.
It is the Fourier transform of the potential at the momentum transfer q=k′−k\mathbf q = \mathbf k' - \mathbf kq=k′−k,
with q=2ksin⁡(θ/2)q = 2k\sin(\theta/2)q=2ksin(θ/2). This is how the form factors of §M2.2 enter cross sections. Chapters 4
and 5 develop both forms.

Operator form. Chapter 4 writes the same equations with the free resolvent
G0(±)(E)=(E−H0±iε)−1G_0^{(\pm)}(E) = (E - H_0 \pm i\varepsilon)^{-1}G0(±)​(E)=(E−H0​±iε)−1 (C&H §4.1.1). In coordinate space
E−H0=(ℏ2/2μ)(∇2+k2)E - H_0 = (\hbar^2/2\mu)(\nabla^2 + k^2)E−H0​=(ℏ2/2μ)(∇2+k2), so

⟨r∣G0(±)(E)∣r′⟩=2μℏ2 G(±)(r−r′)=−2μℏ2 e±ik∣r−r′∣4π∣r−r′∣,(M2.36)\langle\mathbf r|G_0^{(\pm)}(E)|\mathbf r'\rangle = \frac{2\mu}{\hbar^2}\,G^{(\pm)}(\mathbf r - \mathbf r') = -\frac{2\mu}{\hbar^2}\,\frac{e^{\pm ik|\mathbf r - \mathbf r'|}}{4\pi|\mathbf r - \mathbf r'|} , \tag{M2.36} ⟨r∣G0(±)​(E)∣r′⟩=ℏ22μ​G(±)(r−r′)=−ℏ22μ​4π∣r−r′∣e±ik∣r−r′∣​,(M2.36)

and the +iε+i\varepsilon+iε added to the energy is the same as the +iε+i\varepsilon+iε added to k2k^2k2 above.

Partial waves. Expanding (M2.32) in spherical harmonics (C&H §4.8.1) separates it into radial
Green’s functions:

G(+)(r−r′)=∑l,mgl(r,r′)rr′ Ylm(r^) Ylm∗(r^′),gl(r,r′)=−1k j^l(kr<) h^l(+)(kr>),(M2.37)G^{(+)}(\mathbf r - \mathbf r') = \sum_{l,m}\frac{g_l(r, r')}{rr'}\,Y_{lm}(\hat{\mathbf r})\,Y_{lm}^*(\hat{\mathbf r}'),\qquad g_l(r, r') = -\frac{1}{k}\,\hat j_l(kr_<)\,\hat h_l^{(+)}(kr_>) , \tag{M2.37} G(+)(r−r′)=l,m∑​rr′gl​(r,r′)​Ylm​(r^)Ylm∗​(r^′),gl​(r,r′)=−k1​j^​l​(kr<​)h^l(+)​(kr>​),(M2.37)

where r<r_<r<​ and r>r_>r>​ are the smaller and the larger of rrr and r′r'r′. The radial Green’s function
glg_lgl​ solves the free radial equation (2.5) with a source δ(r−r′)\delta(r - r')δ(r−r′). It is regular at the
origin, outgoing at infinity, and its slope jumps by 1 at r=r′r = r'r=r′ because of the Wronskian (2.25).
It is the one-dimensional construction (M2.25), done for each partial wave. The notebook sums
(M2.37) over lll with the addition theorem (M1.13) and recovers (M2.32) to ten digits.

M2.7 The ±iε prescription and the Sokhotski–Plemelj formula

The iεi\varepsiloniε of §M2.6 can also be handled on the real axis. Split

1x∓iε=xx2+ε2±i εx2+ε2.(M2.38)\frac{1}{x \mp i\varepsilon} = \frac{x}{x^2 + \varepsilon^2} \pm i\,\frac{\varepsilon}{x^2 + \varepsilon^2} . \tag{M2.38} x∓iε1​=x2+ε2x​±ix2+ε2ε​.(M2.38)

The imaginary part is π\piπ times the Lorentzian of (M2.2), which tends to πδ(x)\pi\delta(x)πδ(x). The real
part equals 1/x1/x1/x except within about ε\varepsilonε of the origin, where it is cut off
antisymmetrically, so inside an integral it tends to the principal value. Together they give the
Sokhotski–Plemelj formula:

lim⁡ε→0+1x∓iε=P1x±iπ δ(x),P ⁣∫f(x)x dx≡lim⁡η→0+[∫−∞−η+∫η∞]f(x)x dx.(M2.39)\lim_{\varepsilon\to0^+}\frac{1}{x \mp i\varepsilon} = P\frac{1}{x} \pm i\pi\,\delta(x),\qquad P\!\int\frac{f(x)}{x}\,dx \equiv \lim_{\eta\to0^+}\left[\int_{-\infty}^{-\eta} + \int_{\eta}^{\infty}\right]\frac{f(x)}{x}\,dx . \tag{M2.39} ε→0+lim​x∓iε1​=Px1​±iπδ(x),P∫xf(x)​dx≡η→0+lim​[∫−∞−η​+∫η∞​]xf(x)​dx.(M2.39)

In the contour language of §M2.4, take the upper sign. Integrating along the real axis with the pole
just above it, at x=iεx = i\varepsilonx=iε, is the same as integrating with the pole at 0 and a small
semicircle that passes below it. The two straight pieces give the principal value. The semicircle
goes halfway around the pole counterclockwise and contributes half of 2πi2\pi i2πi times the residue,
iπf(0)i\pi f(0)iπf(0).

To compute a principal value numerically, subtract the singularity:

P ⁣∫abf(x)x−x0 dx=∫abf(x)−f(x0)x−x0 dx+f(x0)ln⁡∣b−x0a−x0∣.(M2.40)P\!\int_a^b\frac{f(x)}{x - x_0}\,dx = \int_a^b\frac{f(x) - f(x_0)}{x - x_0}\,dx + f(x_0)\ln\left|\frac{b - x_0}{a - x_0}\right| . \tag{M2.40} P∫ab​x−x0​f(x)​dx=∫ab​x−x0​f(x)−f(x0​)​dx+f(x0​)ln∣∣∣∣∣​a−x0​b−x0​​∣∣∣∣∣​.(M2.40)

The new integrand is smooth (it tends to f′(x0)f'(x_0)f′(x0​) at x0x_0x0​), so any quadrature rule works. This is
scatlib.fourier.principal_value. The test suite checks it against
P ⁣∫e−t2/(t−x) dt=−2π F(x)P\!\int e^{-t^2}/(t - x)\,dt = -2\sqrt\pi\,F(x)P∫e−t2/(t−x)dt=−2π​F(x), where FFF is Dawson’s integral.

Animation M2.2 follows the limit for f(x)=e−(x−1/2)2f(x) = e^{-(x - 1/2)^2}f(x)=e−(x−1/2)2. By (M2.40),
P ⁣∫f/x dx=1.504588P\!\int f/x\,dx = 1.504588P∫f/xdx=1.504588, and πf(0)=2.446675\pi f(0) = 2.446675πf(0)=2.446675. At ε=0.01\varepsilon = 0.01ε=0.01 the integral
I(ε)=∫f(x)/(x−iε) dxI(\varepsilon) = \int f(x)/(x - i\varepsilon)\,dxI(ε)=∫f(x)/(x−iε)dx is 1.480372+2.426393 i1.480372 + 2.426393\,i1.480372+2.426393i. Both parts converge
only linearly in ε\varepsilonε, as expected for a Lorentzian (§M2.1).

shrinks from 1 to 0.01. Right: I(ε)=∫f(x)/(x−iε) dxI(\varepsilon) = \int f(x)/(x - i\varepsilon)\,dxI(ε)=∫f(x)/(x−iε)dx for
f=e−(x−1/2)2f = e^{-(x - 1/2)^2}f=e−(x−1/2)2. The real part tends to P ⁣∫f/x dxP\!\int f/x\,dxP∫f/xdx, the imaginary part to πf(0)\pi f(0)πf(0).
(Notebook §M2.7.)

In scattering theory. Applied to the free resolvent, (M2.39) reads

1E−H0+iε=P1E−H0−iπ δ(E−H0).(M2.41)\frac{1}{E - H_0 + i\varepsilon} = P\frac{1}{E - H_0} - i\pi\,\delta(E - H_0) . \tag{M2.41} E−H0​+iε1​=PE−H0​1​−iπδ(E−H0​).(M2.41)

The principal part is the standing-wave Green’s function GPG^PGP of (M2.33), times 2μ/ℏ22\mu/\hbar^22μ/ℏ2. The
delta-function part, −1πIm G0(+)-\frac{1}{\pi}\mathrm{Im}\,G_0^{(+)}−π1​ImG0(+)​, is proportional to sin⁡kr/r\sin kr/rsinkr/r and contains
only states with energy exactly EEE: it puts intermediate states on the energy shell. Fermi’s golden
rule, the optical theorem and the imaginary part of the TTT-matrix all come from this term. Using
GPG^PGP instead of G(+)G^{(+)}G(+) in the Lippmann–Schwinger equation gives standing-wave solutions and the
real reactance matrix KKK. For a single channel, K=tan⁡δK = \tan\deltaK=tanδ and
S=(1+iK)/(1−iK)S = (1 + iK)/(1 - iK)S=(1+iK)/(1−iK) (Chapter 4).

M2.8 Causality and dispersion relations

Causality makes response functions analytic. Suppose a system responds linearly to a force,
x(t)=∫χ(t−t′) F(t′) dt′x(t) = \int\chi(t - t')\,F(t')\,dt'x(t)=∫χ(t−t′)F(t′)dt′. Causality, meaning no response before the force acts, requires
χ(τ)=0\chi(\tau) = 0χ(τ)=0 for τ<0\tau < 0τ<0. With the time dependence e−iωte^{-i\omega t}e−iωt, the frequency response is

χ(ω)=∫0∞χ(τ) eiωτ dτ.(M2.42)\chi(\omega) = \int_0^\infty\chi(\tau)\,e^{i\omega\tau}\,d\tau . \tag{M2.42} χ(ω)=∫0∞​χ(τ)eiωτdτ.(M2.42)

For complex ω\omegaω with Im ω>0\mathrm{Im}\,\omega > 0Imω>0, the factor eiωτe^{i\omega\tau}eiωτ decays, because only
τ>0\tau > 0τ>0 contributes. The integral converges, and χ(ω)\chi(\omega)χ(ω) is analytic in the upper half of
the complex ω\omegaω plane.

The Kramers–Kronig relations. Suppose also that χ→0\chi \to 0χ→0 as ∣ω∣→∞|\omega| \to \infty∣ω∣→∞. For a point
ω+iε\omega + i\varepsilonω+iε just above the real axis, Cauchy’s integral formula, with the contour closed in
the upper half plane, gives
χ(ω)=12πi∫χ(ω′)/(ω′−ω−iε) dω′\chi(\omega) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int\chi(\omega')/(\omega' - \omega - i\varepsilon)\,d\omega'χ(ω)=2πi1​∫χ(ω′)/(ω′−ω−iε)dω′.
Insert (M2.39) and solve for χ(ω)\chi(\omega)χ(ω):
χ(ω)=1iπP ⁣∫χ(ω′)/(ω′−ω) dω′\chi(\omega) = \frac{1}{i\pi}P\!\int\chi(\omega')/(\omega' - \omega)\,d\omega'χ(ω)=iπ1​P∫χ(ω′)/(ω′−ω)dω′. The real and
imaginary parts of this equation are

Re χ(ω)=1πP ⁣∫−∞∞Im χ(ω′)ω′−ω dω′,Im χ(ω)=−1πP ⁣∫−∞∞Re χ(ω′)ω′−ω dω′.(M2.43)\mathrm{Re}\,\chi(\omega) = \frac{1}{\pi}P\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{Im}\,\chi(\omega')}{\omega' - \omega}\,d\omega',\qquad \mathrm{Im}\,\chi(\omega) = -\frac{1}{\pi}P\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{Re}\,\chi(\omega')}{\omega' - \omega}\,d\omega' . \tag{M2.43} Reχ(ω)=π1​P∫−∞∞​ω′−ωImχ(ω′)​dω′,Imχ(ω)=−π1​P∫−∞∞​ω′−ωReχ(ω′)​dω′.(M2.43)

The dispersive (real) and absorptive (imaginary) parts of a causal response are not independent:
either one determines the other. Kramers and Kronig found this for the refractive index of light,
where it links refraction to absorption.

Example. The damped oscillator x¨+γx˙+ω02x=F\ddot x + \gamma\dot x + \omega_0^2x = Fx¨+γx˙+ω02​x=F has

χ(ω)=1ω02−ω2−iγω,(M2.44)\chi(\omega) = \frac{1}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 - i\gamma\omega} , \tag{M2.44} χ(ω)=ω02​−ω2−iγω1​,(M2.44)

whose poles, at ω=−iγ/2±ω02−γ2/4\omega = -i\gamma/2 \pm \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \gamma^2/4}ω=−iγ/2±ω02​−γ2/4​, both lie in the lower half
plane. For ω0=1\omega_0 = 1ω0​=1 and γ=0.3\gamma = 0.3γ=0.3, (M2.43) evaluated with (M2.40) on ∣ω∣≤300|\omega| \le 300∣ω∣≤300
reconstructs each part from the other to 3×10−73\times10^{-7}3×10−7 (Fig. M2.7a).

A preview of Chapter 10: the threshold anomaly. The optical potential of Chapter 7 is complex,
U=−[V(E)+iW(E)] f(r)U = -[V(E) + iW(E)]\,f(r)U=−[V(E)+iW(E)]f(r), and its absorptive part W>0W > 0W>0 removes flux into reaction channels.
Causality of the underlying many-body dynamics makes V+iWV + iWV+iW, as a function of the energy, analytic
in the upper half of the complex EEE plane. The part of VVV generated by the coupling to the reaction
channels therefore obeys

ΔV(E)=1πP ⁣∫W(E′)E′−E dE′.(M2.45)\Delta V(E) = \frac{1}{\pi}P\!\int\frac{W(E')}{E' - E}\,dE' . \tag{M2.45} ΔV(E)=π1​P∫E′−EW(E′)​dE′.(M2.45)

Because WWW does not vanish at high energy, (M2.45) is used in a subtracted form, referred to an
energy EsE_sEs​:

ΔV(E)=ΔV(Es)+E−Esπ P ⁣∫W(E′)(E′−Es)(E′−E) dE′.(M2.46)\Delta V(E) = \Delta V(E_s) + \frac{E - E_s}{\pi}\,P\!\int\frac{W(E')}{(E' - E_s)(E' - E)}\,dE' . \tag{M2.46} ΔV(E)=ΔV(Es​)+πE−Es​​P∫(E′−Es​)(E′−E)W(E′)​dE′.(M2.46)

Figure M2.7b uses a schematic model of the kind introduced by Mahaux, Ngô and Satchler. WWW rises
linearly from zero at 0.9 VB0.9\,V_B0.9VB​ to W0W_0W0​ at 1.1 VB1.1\,V_B1.1VB​, where VBV_BVB​ is the Coulomb barrier, and stays
constant up to 60 VB60\,V_B60VB​; the reference point is Es=0.2 VBE_s = 0.2\,V_BEs​=0.2VB​ with ΔV(Es)=0\Delta V(E_s) = 0ΔV(Es​)=0. Where the
absorption switches on, ΔV\Delta VΔV develops a peak, 0.975 W00.975\,W_00.975W0​ at E=VBE = V_BE=VB​. Above 1.78 VB1.78\,V_B1.78VB​ it
turns negative and keeps decreasing logarithmically. Near the barrier the real potential is therefore
deeper than its high-energy trend suggests. This is the threshold anomaly, seen for example in
the elastic scattering of ¹⁶O + ²⁰⁸Pb near the barrier. The extra attraction lowers the Coulomb barrier and enhances
fusion below the barrier (Chapter 14).

Figure M2.7. (a) Kramers–Kronig relations for a damped oscillator (ω0=1\omega_0 = 1ω0​=1,
γ=0.3\gamma = 0.3γ=0.3). Lines: the exact Re χ\mathrm{Re}\,\chiReχ and Im χ\mathrm{Im}\,\chiImχ. Circles: each part
computed from the other with (M2.43). (b) The threshold anomaly in a schematic model. An absorptive
part W(E)W(E)W(E) that switches on around the barrier produces, through the subtracted dispersion relation
(M2.46), a peak in the real part ΔV(E)\Delta V(E)ΔV(E). (Notebook §M2.8.)

Summary

  • The delta function is the limit, inside integrals, of nascent delta functions. The key identities
    are ∫eikx dk=2πδ(x)\int e^{ikx}\,dk = 2\pi\delta(x)∫eikxdk=2πδ(x); δ(g(x))\delta(g(x))δ(g(x)) picks up a factor 1/∣g′∣1/|g'|1/∣g′∣ at each zero; and
    ∇2(1/r)=−4πδ3(r)\nabla^2(1/r) = -4\pi\delta^3(\mathbf r)∇2(1/r)=−4πδ3(r).
  • With f~(q)=∫e−iq⋅rf d3r\tilde f(\mathbf q) = \int e^{-i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r}f\,d^3rf~​(q)=∫e−iq⋅rfd3r, a spherical function has a sine
    transform. A form factor shows the size of a nucleus in its minima, the surface in its fall-off and
    the rms radius in its slope at q=0q = 0q=0.
  • Continuum states are normalized to delta functions, and only the asymptotic amplitude matters. In a
    box, levels shift by −δ/Rbox-\delta/R_{\rm box}−δ/Rbox​, the density of states changes by
    1π dδ/dk\frac{1}{\pi}\,d\delta/dkπ1​dδ/dk, and counting states gives Levinson’s theorem.
  • Residues and Jordan’s lemma evaluate Fourier-type integrals: close the contour on the side where
    eiqre^{iqr}eiqr decays.
  • A Green’s function is the response to a point source, and the boundary condition selects it. The
    Lippmann–Schwinger equation is the Schrödinger equation with the scattering boundary conditions
    built in; solved numerically, it gives rrr and ttt directly.
  • G(±)=−e±ikr/4πrG^{(\pm)} = -e^{\pm ikr}/4\pi rG(±)=−e±ikr/4πr follow from k2±iεk^2 \pm i\varepsilonk2±iε, and GP=−cos⁡kr/4πrG^P = -\cos kr/4\pi rGP=−coskr/4πr is
    their average. The scattering amplitude is
    f=−14π∫e−ik′⋅r Uψ(+) d3rf = -\frac{1}{4\pi}\int e^{-i\mathbf k'\cdot\mathbf r}\,U\psi^{(+)}\,d^3rf=−4π1​∫e−ik′⋅rUψ(+)d3r.
  • 1/(x∓iε)→P(1/x)±iπδ(x)1/(x \mp i\varepsilon) \to P(1/x) \pm i\pi\delta(x)1/(x∓iε)→P(1/x)±iπδ(x). Principal values are computed by subtracting
    the singularity.
  • Causality makes response functions analytic in the upper half plane, and their real and imaginary
    parts are then related by the Kramers–Kronig relations. For the optical potential this gives the
    dispersion relation behind the threshold anomaly.
